narratives.name: Governance Journey from Basic Access Control to Autonomous Compliance
narratives.description: Progressive governance implementation through RBAC, analytics, credential security, and self-service portal capabilities.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations begin their governance journey by establishing basic organizational boundaries and team-based permissions through the platform gateway, configuring initial analytics dashboards to capture job execution telemetry, and storing credentials locally within the automation controller database with standard encryption.

Governance matures as team administrators gain delegated authority to manage their own membership and permissions, analytics quantify ROI through customizable metrics and savings projections, the self-service portal publishes approved automation services with approval workflows and ITSM integration, and external vault systems provide dynamic credential retrieval at job execution time.

Advanced governance reaches full maturity with custom RBAC roles enforcing organization-specific permission boundaries, zero-trust credential operations using OIDC-issued short-lived JWT tokens scoped to individual job executions, business intelligence integration feeding automation analytics into enterprise reporting tools, and a self-service marketplace enabling autonomous automation consumption across the enterprise with comprehensive audit and compliance reporting.

narratives.name: RBAC Governance Maturity Through Platform Gateway
narratives.description: Progressive governance from centralized administration to fully delegated self-service with custom roles.

narrativeContexts.context: Governance begins with a centralized administration model where system administrators manually configure users and permissions through the platform gateway, establishing foundational organizational boundaries and identifying which teams need access to which automation resources.

As the platform matures, team-based permissions replace individual assignments, team administrators gain delegated authority to manage their own membership, and identity provider integration automates team membership through LDAP group mapping or OIDC claims, significantly reducing administrative overhead while maintaining control.

Fully mature governance features custom RBAC roles with organization-specific permission sets, self-service resource creation governed by organizational boundaries, and comprehensive audit reporting that tracks permission assignments and access patterns across all platform services with automated compliance validation.

narratives.name: Mapping Organizational Structure to Platform Permissions
narratives.description: How AAP organization and team hierarchy enables delegated governance.

narrativeContexts.context: Effective automation governance requires mapping organizational structures into the platform's permission model so that teams can operate autonomously within clear boundaries, and the AAP organization and team hierarchy provides the structural foundation for this delegation model.

AAP organizations provide top-level logical isolation where each business unit or functional area operates with independent teams, resources, and administrators, while teams within organizations group users sharing common permissions with role inheritance automatically applying to all members.

Organizations implementing delegated team administration with self-service permission workflows achieve significantly faster onboarding and higher user satisfaction compared to centralized administration models, while maintaining equivalent or better security posture through automated permission reviews and audit logging.

The team-to-organization mapping approach in AAP enables a governance model that balances organizational control with team autonomy, scaling from simple centralized administration to fully delegated self-service as governance maturity progresses.

narratives.name: From Persistent Secrets to Zero-Trust Credential Operations
narratives.description: Progressive elimination of credential exposure through vault integration and OIDC token issuance.

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise automation platforms manage hundreds of credentials granting access to production infrastructure, cloud APIs, and databases, creating significant security exposure when long-lived secrets are stored in platform databases or shared across jobs without proper scoping.

Progressively eliminate persistent credential storage by implementing external vault integration with dynamic credential retrieval, and ultimately achieve zero-trust credential operations where every job receives uniquely scoped, short-lived tokens that automatically expire after execution completes.

Configure OIDC Identity Provider on AAP gateway issuing JWT tokens scoped to individual job executions with claims identifying job ID, user, and organization, then configure HashiCorp Vault policies that validate these claims to restrict secret access by job context.

Zero-trust credential operations eliminate persistent secret storage, reduce breach exposure windows from months to minutes, provide comprehensive audit trails for compliance reporting, and enable anomaly detection to identify unusual credential access patterns automatically.

activities.name: Design RBAC Organizational Model
activities.description: Map business units to AAP organizations and define team permission inheritance.

narratives.name: Designing RBAC Organizational Model for AAP
narratives.description: Translating business unit structure into platform RBAC model.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations deploying AAP need to translate their business unit structure into the platform's RBAC model before users can be granted appropriate access, but without careful planning the permission model becomes an administrative bottleneck or a security gap.

Design an organizational mapping that aligns AAP organizations to business units or regulatory boundaries, defines team structures within each organization, and establishes the initial permission model that will scale from basic administration to delegated self-service.

Analyze the organizational chart to identify natural isolation boundaries, create AAP organizations for each major business unit, define teams reflecting functional roles within each organization, and document the permission model including which built-in roles apply to which resource types per team.

A documented RBAC organizational model provides the foundation for team-based permission inheritance, enabling subsequent delegation and self-service configuration while maintaining governance visibility through platform gateway.

activities.name: Implement Gateway RBAC Policies
activities.description: Configure organizations, teams, roles, and identity provider integration through gateway.

narratives.name: Implementing Gateway RBAC Policies
narratives.description: Configuring team-based RBAC through the platform gateway.

narrativeContexts.context: The RBAC organizational model has been designed but not yet implemented, and users still rely on system administrators for all permission management through the platform gateway, creating bottlenecks for onboarding and resource access.

Implement the designed RBAC model by creating organizations and teams in AAP through the platform gateway, configuring identity provider group mapping for automated membership, and applying role-based permissions across controller, hub, and EDA controller.

Create organizations specifying names and default execution environments, define teams within each organization, configure LDAP/SAML/OIDC group mapping to automate team membership, apply built-in roles (Admin, Execute, Use, Read) to resources per team, and validate permission inheritance through end-to-end testing.

Team-based RBAC policies are operational through platform gateway with automated membership via identity provider integration, reducing administrative overhead while establishing consistent access control across all platform services.

activities.name: Enable Delegated Team Administration
activities.description: Assign team administrator roles and configure self-service permission management.

narratives.name: Enabling Delegated Team Administration
narratives.description: Transitioning from centralized to delegated team-level permission management.

narrativeContexts.context: Team-based RBAC is operational but all team membership and permission changes still require system administrator involvement, creating a bottleneck as the number of teams and users grows.
Enable team leads to independently manage their own team membership and resource permissions within defined boundaries, while organization administrators maintain cross-team governance oversight.

Assign team administrator roles to designated team leads, configure organization-level administrator roles for cross-team oversight, document delegation boundaries specifying what team admins can and cannot modify, and establish self-service permission request workflows.

Delegated administration reduces system administrator workload, accelerates team onboarding, and enables teams to self-manage their permission model within governance boundaries enforced by the platform gateway.

narratives.description: Advanced RBAC governance with custom roles and automated compliance monitoring.

narrativeContexts.context: Organizations with mature RBAC models need custom roles beyond built-in permissions, along with automated detection of overprivileged access and comprehensive audit reporting for compliance requirements.

Implement custom RBAC roles, configure organization-level self-service resource creation, establish automated permission reviews, and deploy audit reporting that tracks permission assignments and access patterns.

Create custom roles defining tailored permission sets per organization, configure organization-level Add permissions for governed self-service, implement automated scripts identifying overprivileged users and stale access, and configure SIEM integration forwarding RBAC audit logs from platform gateway.

Comprehensive RBAC governance with custom roles, automated compliance monitoring, and audit-ready reporting demonstrates policy adherence across all platform services and enables proactive identification of permission risks.

activities.name: Configure Vault Credential Integration
activities.description: Implement external vault connectivity with credential lookup plugins.

narratives.name: Configuring Vault Credential Integration
narratives.description: Implementing external vault connectivity for dynamic credential retrieval.

narrativeContexts.context: Credentials stored in the automation controller database create security risk from persistent secret exposure, and manual credential rotation introduces human error and compliance gaps.
Integrate external vault systems (HashiCorp Vault, CyberArk, Azure Key Vault) to provide dynamic credential retrieval at job execution time, eliminating persistent secret storage.

Configure credential type in controller specifying Vault server URL and authentication method, create custom credential types mapping vault paths to job template variables, test credential injection by launching job templates, and configure audit logging through vault.

Dynamic credential retrieval from external vault systems eliminates persistent secret storage, enables vault-managed rotation without controller changes, and provides comprehensive audit trails for compliance reporting.

activities.name: Implement OIDC Credential Issuance
activities.description: Configure AAP as OIDC identity provider for HashiCorp Vault enabling JWT tokens.

narratives.name: Implementing OIDC Credential Issuance
narratives.description: Configuring AAP as OIDC identity provider for zero-trust credential operations.

narrativeContexts.context: External vault integration retrieves secrets dynamically but still relies on long-lived authentication credentials stored in the controller to authenticate to the vault, creating a residual security exposure window.
Eliminate all long-lived credentials by configuring AAP as a native OIDC identity provider that issues short-lived, job-scoped JWT tokens for vault authentication with automatic revocation.

Configure AAP gateway as OIDC issuer with signing keys and token lifetime policies, configure HashiCorp Vault JWT auth method trusting AAP as identity provider, create vault policies mapping OIDC claims to secret access paths, and validate end-to-end flow.

OIDC-based credential issuance eliminates all persistent credential storage, reduces breach exposure windows from months to minutes, and provides fine-grained audit trails linking every secret access to a specific job, user, and organization.

Conduct a comprehensive inventory of all credential types, documenting storage locations, rotation status, and identifying which credentials are suitable for OIDC/Vault migration.

narratives.description: Completing the migration to fully zero-trust credential management.

narrativeContexts.context: OIDC credential issuance is operational for critical workflows but some credential types remain outside the zero-trust model, and compliance reporting requires manual evidence collection.
Complete the migration of all production credentials to OIDC/Vault integration, implement anomaly detection for credential access patterns, and establish automated compliance reporting.

Migrate remaining production credential paths to OIDC/Vault with no persistent secrets, configure automated rotation schedules, implement anomaly detection rules, document and test break-glass procedures, and deploy automated compliance reporting templates.

Zero-trust credential operations are fully established with no persistent secrets, automated anomaly detection providing continuous monitoring, and compliance reports generating machine-readable audit evidence.

activities.name: Automate Governance Remediation
activities.description: Implement automated detection and remediation of governance violations.

narratives.description: Self-healing governance through automated detection and remediation.

narrativeContexts.context: Governance violations including unauthorized RBAC changes, credential rotation lapses, and configuration drift are detected through monitoring but require manual investigation and remediation.

Implement automated governance remediation that detects violations through event-driven monitoring, classifies them by severity, and either auto-remediates or escalates with documented investigation procedures.

Configure anomaly detection rules for credential access patterns and RBAC changes, implement GitOps reconciliation for unauthorized configuration drift, establish tiered remediation workflows, and integrate with audit logging for compliance evidence.

Self-healing governance operates within defined boundaries with automated remediation for known violation patterns, event-driven responses to anomalies, and comprehensive audit trails demonstrating continuous compliance enforcement.
